fallback.ledeTemplate: {{title}} defines a system-level rule that must be visible in design, code, content, accessibility, and agent output.
columns: {{title}} clarifies what the system should emphasize or prevent.
The rule is semantic before it is visual.
The same foundation must work in mobile driver flows and desktop fleet operations.
Agents should be able to read the rule and produce consistent UI decisions.

Energy.lede: When visual intensity appears in Design System, it always carries meaning. Energy lets drivers and fleet managers understand what is actionable, successful, risky, broken, or simply structural.
columns: Energy translates product priority into color, emphasis, rhythm, and status.
Energy is never decoration. It communicates intent, hierarchy, and feedback.
Energy keeps dashboards calm while making operational exceptions unmistakable.
Energy makes the product learnable because the same signal means the same thing everywhere.

Voice.lede: Voice defines how Design System writes, labels, explains, repairs, confirms, and escalates. It combines Edenred Black display/title/numeral typography with Ubuntu body/UI text.
columns: Labels name the object precisely before describing the action.
Guidance appears before risk, not after the user fails.
Repair copy explains what happened and what can be done next.
Confirmation copy records consequence, owner, and next state.

Frame.lede: Frame governs all spatial relationships: page rhythm, panels, density, grid, responsive behavior, and what belongs together.
columns: Every gap, padding, and grouping decision comes from a shared spatial scale.
Frame separates primary work from supporting context.
Density is declared at the surface level and inherited by components.
Frame prevents ad-hoc layout fixes from becoming design language.

Depth.lede: Depth defines the spatial metaphor of the interface: how surfaces stack, how overlays focus attention, and how elevation communicates hierarchy.
columns: Depth separates canvas, raised content, floating controls, overlays, and critical feedback.
Elevation uses tokenized shadows and z-index ranges instead of arbitrary stacking.
Maps, sheets, menus, and dashboards use the same spatial grammar.
Depth tells users what is persistent, temporary, contextual, or blocking.

Momentum.lede: Momentum governs animation and transition so movement explains cause, continuity, status, and system activity without becoming decoration.
columns: Durations map to micro-interactions, transitions, choreography, and continuous feedback.
Easing distinguishes elements entering, exiting, moving continuously, or changing state.
Stagger organizes dense content like dashboards and route alternatives.
Reduced motion preserves meaning when translation, scale, or continuous animation is minimized.

State.lede: State defines which interaction states exist, how they combine, and which state wins when several conditions happen at once.
columns: Hover, focus, pressed, selected, loading, disabled, error, and success are formal states.
Disabled and loading suppress conflicting affordances before components render.
Focus and error can coexist because one explains navigation and the other explains validation.
State maps visual behavior to assistive technology semantics.

Iconography.lede: Iconography defines functional glyph rules: grid, size, category, naming, color, and accessible labeling.
columns: Icons are functional glyphs, not decorative art.
Material Symbols are consumed through semantic categories and tokenized size/color roles.
Icon-only actions require accessible names and predictable hit targets.
Missing icons should fail visibly during documentation and implementation.
